title: The Rooftop Farmers of Medellín
paragraphs: On a flat concrete roof in the hillside neighbourhood of Manrique, in north-eastern Medellín, Luz Marina Restrepo is checking her lettuces. Five years ago, the space above her family's house was used only for drying clothes and storing broken furniture. Today it is covered with more than forty wooden boxes full of vegetables, herbs and even a few small lemon trees. "I never imagined I would become a farmer in the middle of the city," she says, laughing. "My grandparents worked the land in Antioquia, but I grew up surrounded by bricks."

Luz Marina is one of a growing number of residents who have turned unused roofs and terraces into small productive gardens. The idea is not new, since urban agriculture has existed for centuries, but in recent years it has been encouraged by community organisations, universities and, in some cases, local authorities. Workshops are offered in which people learn how to build raised beds, make compost from kitchen waste and collect rainwater in recycled containers.

The benefits are not only economic, although these matter. A family that grows its own tomatoes, onions, coriander and beans can save a noticeable amount of money each month, especially when food prices rise. Some gardeners also sell their surplus to neighbours or exchange it for other products. "Last year we swapped our spinach for eggs from a woman two streets away," Luz Marina explains. "Nobody paid a single peso."

Experts point out that rooftop gardens can also help the city itself. Plants absorb part of the heat that concrete would otherwise store, so houses with green roofs tend to stay cooler during the hottest hours of the day. Gardens also slow down rainwater, which reduces the pressure on drains during heavy storms. If thousands of roofs were covered in this way, some researchers believe, the effect on local temperatures could be measurable.

However, rooftop farming is not without its difficulties. Not every building is strong enough to support the weight of wet soil, and engineers warn that structures should be checked before large gardens are installed. Water can be another problem in dry months, and pests such as aphids spread quickly when plants are grown close together. Beginners are often disappointed when their first harvest is smaller than expected. "The yield in the first season was terrible," admits Andrés Gil, a young gardener who started his project during the pandemic. "I had to learn that soil is alive, and you have to feed it."

Perhaps the most surprising result, however, is social. Many participants say that the gardens have changed their relationship with their neighbours. Children who had never seen a seed germinate now help with watering, and older residents who grew up in the countryside have become respected teachers. For Luz Marina, this is the real harvest. "We started growing food," she says, "but in the end we grew a community."

title: Bogotá Firms Test the Four-Day Week
paragraphs: A group of small and medium-sized companies in Bogotá has completed a six-month trial in which employees worked four days a week instead of five, without any reduction in salary. The results, which were presented at a business forum last Thursday, have been described by the organisers as "encouraging but not conclusive".

Twenty-three firms took part in the experiment, ranging from a software developer with fifteen employees to a logistics company with more than two hundred. Each company was allowed to design its own model. Some closed their offices on Fridays, while others divided staff into two teams so that customers could still be served every weekday. The only condition was that total working hours had to fall by around twenty per cent.

According to the final report, most participating companies said that productivity had either stayed the same or improved. Staff surveys showed that levels of stress and exhaustion had fallen, and that fewer people had taken sick leave than in the same period the previous year. Several managers also noted that meetings had become shorter and more focused. "When you only have four days, you stop wasting time on things that don't matter," said Catalina Ospina, director of a marketing agency that took part.

Not everyone was so positive, however. Two companies abandoned the trial after three months, explaining that they had been unable to meet their clients' deadlines. In the logistics sector, where trucks have to be loaded and unloaded every day, managers found it difficult to organise shifts without hiring extra workers. Some employees also admitted that their four working days had become longer and more intense, which partly cancelled out the benefits of the extra day off.

Economists who have studied similar programmes in Europe warn against drawing quick conclusions. They point out that companies which volunteer for such trials are often those that are already open to change, so the results may not reflect what would happen in the economy as a whole. "It works well in offices where output can be measured in projects," explained one labour researcher. "It is much harder in hospitals, schools or factories."

Despite these doubts, eighteen of the twenty-three companies have decided to keep the shorter week, at least for now. The organisers hope to launch a second, larger trial next year, which would include businesses in Medellín, Cali and Barranquilla. If that happens, they say, it would provide much more reliable evidence about whether the model can work in Colombia.

title: My Students Started Using AI. Here's What I Learned
paragraphs: When I first noticed that half of my Grade 10 essays sounded exactly the same, I was furious. The sentences were perfectly correct, the vocabulary was impressive, and not a single one of them sounded like a sixteen-year-old from Cali. It didn't take me long to work out what had happened: my students had discovered AI chatbots, and they were using them to write their homework.

My first reaction was to ban them completely. I told the class that any text produced with artificial intelligence would receive a zero, and I started asking students to write everything by hand in the classroom. For a few weeks, this seemed to work. But I soon realised that I was spending all my energy acting like a police officer instead of a teacher, and the atmosphere in the class had become tense and suspicious.

So I decided to try something different. Instead of pretending the technology didn't exist, I brought it into the lesson. In one activity, students asked a chatbot to write a short opinion paragraph, and then they had to find its weaknesses. They were surprised to discover how often the machine gave vague answers, repeated the same ideas, or invented facts that sounded convincing but were completely false. One boy, Samuel, found that it had confidently described a festival in his town that has never existed.

In another activity, they wrote their own first drafts and then used AI only to get feedback on grammar. The rule was simple: the tool could point out mistakes, but it couldn't rewrite their sentences. They had to correct the errors themselves and explain why the new version was better. To my surprise, many students found this genuinely useful, and their writing improved more quickly than in previous years.

I don't want to give the impression that everything has been solved. Some students still try to take shortcuts, and I'm sure a few of them get away with it. I also worry about the students who don't have reliable internet at home, because they can't practise in the same way as their classmates. And honestly, I'm not sure what the rules should be for the final exams, which are still written without any technology.

What I have learned, though, is that banning a tool rarely teaches anyone how to use it wisely. My students are going to live and work in a world full of artificial intelligence. If school doesn't help them to think critically about it, who will? I'd love to hear how other teachers are dealing with this, so leave a comment below and tell me what has worked for you.

title: Why Teenagers Can't Fall Asleep Early
paragraphs: Parents all over the world know the scene. It is eleven o'clock at night, the house is quiet, and a teenager is wide awake, scrolling on a phone or watching videos. The next morning, the same teenager can hardly get out of bed. For a long time, this behaviour was blamed on laziness or bad habits. Scientists now believe that the explanation is, at least partly, biological.

Every human being has an internal clock, known as the circadian rhythm, which tells the body when to feel sleepy and when to feel alert. One of the key signals in this system is melatonin, a hormone that is released in the evening as it gets dark. During adolescence, however, the release of melatonin is delayed. As a result, many teenagers simply do not feel tired until much later than they did as children, often not before eleven o'clock or midnight.

A second process makes the situation worse. Throughout the day, a substance called adenosine gradually builds up in the brain, creating what researchers call "sleep pressure". The more pressure there is, the sleepier we feel. Studies suggest that in teenagers this pressure builds up more slowly, which means they can stay awake longer in the evening without feeling exhausted.

The problem is that school timetables do not take this biology into account. Most experts recommend that teenagers should sleep between eight and ten hours a night. If a student falls asleep at midnight and has to get up at half past five to catch a school bus, as many do in Latin American cities, they will get less than six hours. Over weeks and months, this lack of sleep has been linked to poorer concentration, lower marks, changes in mood and even a higher risk of accidents.

Screens do not help either. The light from phones and tablets can delay melatonin further, and the content itself, from messages to games and social media, keeps the brain active. For this reason, doctors often advise families to switch off devices at least an hour before bed and to keep phones out of the bedroom.

Some school districts, particularly in the United States, have experimented with starting classes later in the morning. In one well-known study, when the start time was moved later by almost an hour, students slept about half an hour more on average, and their attendance improved. Critics argue that later starts create problems for transport and for working parents. Still, the research sends a clear message: when a teenager says they cannot sleep, they may be telling the truth.

title: Living With Visitors: A Cartagena Guide Speaks
paragraphs: Mauricio Herrera has worked as a tour guide in Cartagena's historic walled city for almost twenty years. He speaks four languages, knows the story behind almost every balcony, and has watched the city become one of the most visited destinations in South America. We asked him about the advantages and the costs of that success.

Q: How has the old city changed since you started working as a guide? A: Enormously. When I began, many of the colonial houses were still family homes. You could hear children playing in the streets and neighbours chatting in their doorways in the evening. Now a large number of those houses have been converted into boutique hotels, restaurants or holiday apartments. The buildings are more beautiful than ever, because owners have invested in restoring them, but the neighbourhood feels emptier, if that makes sense. At night it is full of visitors, but very few people actually live there.

Q: Is tourism good for the people of Cartagena? A: It depends on who you ask. Tourism has created thousands of jobs for guides, waiters, drivers, artisans and musicians. My own family has benefited from it. But a lot of the money ends up with big companies, and many of the workers earn very little. Meanwhile, rents in the central neighbourhoods have risen so much that local families have been pushed out to areas much further from the centre. Getsemaní is a good example: it used to be a working-class neighbourhood, and now it is one of the most fashionable places in the city.

Q: What do visitors usually get wrong about the city? A: Many of them only see the walls, the beaches and the nightlife. They don't realise that Cartagena was one of the main ports through which enslaved Africans were brought to the Americas. When I tell them about that history, some people are genuinely shocked. I think a good guide shouldn't only entertain people; we should also help them understand the place they are visiting, including the painful parts.

Q: If you could change one thing about tourism here, what would it be? A: I would want visitors to spend more time, and more money, outside the walled city. There are fantastic community projects in places like San Basilio de Palenque, where people have preserved African traditions, music and even their own language. If more tourists went there with respectful local guides, the benefits would be shared much more fairly.

Q: And what advice would you give to someone visiting for the first time? A: Walk slowly, especially in the heat! Talk to people, eat in small local places, and ask questions. And please, don't haggle aggressively with street vendors over a few hundred pesos. For you it's nothing; for them it might be lunch.

title: Five Weeks with a Language App: An Honest Review
paragraphs: Like millions of people, I have downloaded language apps before and abandoned them within a week. So when I decided to learn Portuguese before a work trip to São Paulo, I promised myself I would use one app, WordWave, every single day for five weeks and then write an honest review. Here is what I found.

Let's start with the positives. The app is beautifully designed and extremely easy to use. Lessons last around ten minutes, which makes them easy to fit into a bus journey or a lunch break. The speech-recognition feature, which asks you to repeat phrases aloud, is surprisingly accurate, and it helped me notice sounds that do not exist in Spanish, such as the nasal vowel in "pão". I also liked the streak counter, which shows how many consecutive days you have studied. It sounds childish, but after twenty days I was genuinely afraid of losing my streak.

As a Spanish speaker, however, I found the beginning frustratingly slow. The first two weeks were full of words like "casa", "mesa" and "obrigado" that I either already knew or could easily guess. There is a placement test, but it seemed to underestimate my level, and I couldn't find a way to skip the easy units without paying for the premium version.

That leads me to my biggest criticism: the price. The free version shows an advertisement after almost every lesson, and some of the most useful features, such as offline lessons, grammar explanations and unlimited mistakes, are only available to subscribers. The premium plan costs about the same as a monthly gym membership, which is not cheap for many learners in Latin America.

Another weakness is that the app focuses heavily on isolated sentences. I learned to say "The boy drinks orange juice" in perfect Portuguese, but when I tried to have a real conversation with a Brazilian colleague on a video call, I struggled to follow her. Real people speak fast, use slang and interrupt each other, something no app has fully managed to imitate.

So, is WordWave worth it? In my opinion, it is an excellent tool for building a daily habit and learning basic vocabulary, especially for complete beginners. But it should be one part of your learning, not all of it. If I had relied on the app alone, I would have arrived in São Paulo able to read a menu but unable to chat over lunch. My final rating: three and a half stars out of five.

title: The Last Batch
paragraphs: The bus left Elena at the bottom of the hill just as the afternoon rain began. She had not been back to San Vicente de Chucurí for six years, and as she climbed the muddy path towards her grandfather's farm, she wondered whether he would even recognise her. In Bogotá she had become someone else: a woman in a grey suit who answered emails at midnight and ate lunch in front of a screen.

Don Aurelio was sitting on the porch, exactly where she had left him, surrounded by the sweet, sour smell of fermenting cacao. He looked smaller than she remembered. "So the engineer has come home," he said, without getting up. "Your mother told me you'd lost your job." Elena felt her face burn. "I didn't lose it, Abuelo. The company closed the office." He nodded slowly, as if the difference did not matter very much.

That evening, over a bowl of soup, he told her the real reason he had asked her to come. A chocolate company from abroad had offered to buy the farm. The money was good, more than he had earned in his whole life, and his knees could no longer manage the steep slopes. "This will be the last batch," he said, pointing towards the wooden boxes where the beans were fermenting under banana leaves. "After that, I sign."

For the next week, Elena worked beside him. She learned to open the yellow pods with a single cut of the machete, to turn the beans so that they fermented evenly, and to spread them out on the drying racks whenever the sun appeared. Her grandfather tasted the beans constantly, like a musician tuning an instrument. "Every farm has its own flavour," he told her. "The soil, the rain, the hands. You can't buy that."

One night, unable to sleep, Elena opened her laptop and started doing what she did best: calculations. She looked up prices for fine-flavour cacao, the cost of a small processing machine and the number of tourists who visited the region each year. By sunrise she had filled ten pages with numbers and arrows. It was not a perfect plan, but it was a beginning.

When she showed it to Don Aurelio, he studied the pages for a long time without saying anything. Then he pushed them back across the table. "I don't understand half of this," he admitted. "But I understand that you would have to stay." Elena looked out at the green hills and the mist rising from the trees, and realised that she had already made her decision.

The last batch was dried, bagged and sold that month, as planned. But the farm was never sold. Two years later, a small wooden sign appeared at the bottom of the hill, with an arrow pointing up the muddy path. It read: "Chocolate Aurelio: visitors welcome."

title: How to Shine in a Video Job Interview
paragraphs: More and more companies now hold the first round of interviews online, and for many candidates, especially those applying to international firms or remote positions, a video call may be the only interview they ever have. Although it may seem easier than meeting face to face, an online interview has its own challenges. Here are some practical steps that will help you make a strong impression.

1. Test your technology in advance. Nothing creates a worse first impression than a candidate who cannot turn on their microphone. At least a day before the interview, download the platform the company is using, check that your camera and microphone work, and make sure you know how to share your screen. If your internet connection is unstable, ask a friend or a local library whether you could borrow a quieter, more reliable space. It is also a good idea to have your phone nearby and fully charged, in case the call drops and you need to reconnect.

2. Think carefully about what the interviewer will see. Position the camera at eye level, so that you are not looking down at it, and sit facing a window or a lamp rather than with the light behind you. Choose a plain background and remove anything that might distract the interviewer, such as piles of laundry or posters. Dress exactly as you would for an in-person interview, from head to toe. You never know when you might need to stand up!

3. Prepare your answers, but don't memorise them. Research the company and the role, and prepare examples from your experience that show your skills. A useful method is to describe a situation, the task you had, the action you took and the result you achieved. However, avoid reading from notes on the screen; interviewers can usually tell when your eyes are moving across a text. Instead, write three or four key words on a sticky note next to the camera.

4. Communicate clearly. There is often a slight delay in video calls, so wait a second before answering to avoid interrupting. Look at the camera, not at your own image, when you speak; this creates the feeling of eye contact. Speak a little more slowly than usual, and if you are being interviewed in English as a second language, don't panic if you need a question repeated. Saying "Sorry, could you repeat that? The connection broke up for a moment" is perfectly acceptable.

5. Finish professionally. At the end, you will probably be asked whether you have any questions. Always have one or two ready, for example about the team or the next steps in the process. Within twenty-four hours, send a short thank-you email. It takes five minutes, and it could be the detail that makes you stand out.

title: Cable Cars and Commuting: Survey Findings
paragraphs: Introduction. This report summarises the findings of a survey carried out by a university research group three years after the opening of the city's first cable car line, which connects four hillside neighbourhoods with the main bus station in the valley. The aim was to find out how the system has affected residents' daily travel, their access to jobs and services, and their perception of the area. A total of 1,200 residents were interviewed, and the results were compared with a similar survey conducted before the line opened.

Travel time. The most significant change concerns travel time. Before the cable car was built, residents of the highest neighbourhood spent an average of 70 minutes travelling to the city centre, usually on informal minibuses along narrow, congested roads. This figure has now fallen to around 35 minutes. Respondents who work night shifts reported the greatest benefit, as public transport had previously been extremely limited after ten o'clock.

Cost. Because the cable car is integrated with the city's bus network, passengers can transfer using a single card. As a result, the average amount spent on transport per household has fallen by approximately 15 per cent. However, a minority of respondents, mainly elderly people and street vendors carrying goods, said they still preferred the minibuses, which stop closer to their homes and allow them to travel with large bags.

Perception and safety. Around two thirds of residents said they felt the image of their neighbourhood had improved since the line opened. Several mentioned that visitors from other parts of the city, and even foreign tourists, now come to enjoy the views. The stations, which include a library and a small community centre, were described as clean and well lit. On the other hand, some respondents expressed concern that rising interest in the area could lead to higher rents.

Limitations. It should be noted that the survey was carried out only among people who live near the stations. Those living further away, who may benefit less, were not included. In addition, the period studied coincided with an economic recovery, so it is difficult to determine to what extent changes in employment were caused by the cable car itself.

Recommendations. Based on these findings, the research group recommends that the city should improve connections between the stations and the more distant streets, for example with small electric buses or safer staircases and paths. It also suggests that a programme to protect long-term tenants should be considered before property prices rise significantly. Finally, a follow-up study should be carried out in five years' time.

title: Running in the Heat: What Happens to Your Body
paragraphs: When the Barranquilla sun is shining and the temperature is above thirty degrees, even a gentle jog can feel like climbing a mountain. Your heart beats faster, your legs feel heavy, and your shirt is soaked within minutes. This is not just a matter of willpower. Exercising in hot conditions forces the body to do two difficult jobs at the same time, and understanding what is going on can help runners stay safe.

When you run, your muscles produce a large amount of heat. To keep its core temperature at around 37 degrees, the body has to get rid of that heat. The main way it does this is by sweating: as sweat evaporates from the skin, it carries heat away. At the same time, more blood is sent to the skin, where it can cool down. The problem is that this blood is no longer available to carry oxygen to the working muscles, so the heart has to beat faster to keep up.

Humidity makes things considerably worse. In very humid air, which is common on the Caribbean coast, sweat cannot evaporate easily. It simply drips off the body without cooling it down. This is why a run at 30 degrees in a dry climate may feel much more comfortable than the same run in a humid one, and why many experienced runners judge conditions by humidity rather than temperature alone.

If the body cannot lose heat quickly enough, the consequences can be serious. Early warning signs include dizziness, headaches, nausea and unusual tiredness. In extreme cases, a runner may develop heatstroke, a medical emergency in which the core temperature rises above 40 degrees and the brain stops working normally. Anyone who becomes confused or stops sweating during exercise in the heat needs immediate medical help.

Fortunately, the human body is remarkably adaptable. Research has shown that after around ten to fourteen days of regular training in hot conditions, the body begins to acclimatise. Athletes start sweating earlier and more heavily, they lose less salt in their sweat, and the volume of their blood increases. As a result, their heart rate during exercise is lower, and they feel more comfortable. This is why professional athletes often travel to hot locations weeks before a major competition.

For ordinary runners, sports scientists offer some simple advice. Train early in the morning or in the evening, when temperatures are lower. Drink regularly, but do not force yourself to drink huge amounts, as too much water can also be dangerous. Wear light, loose clothing, slow down on hot days, and listen to your body. A personal best can always wait for a cooler day.

title: Second-Hand Clothes Are the Future, Not a Trend
paragraphs: Ten years ago, if you told your friends that your jacket came from a second-hand shop, they might have looked at you with pity. Today, they are more likely to ask for the address. In cities from Bogotá to Berlin, buying used clothes has gone from something people did because they had to, to something they do because they want to. Some commentators dismiss this as a passing fashion. I believe they are wrong, and that second-hand shopping should become the normal way we dress.

The first argument is environmental. The fashion industry is responsible for a significant share of global carbon emissions and uses enormous amounts of water. Producing a single pair of jeans, for instance, can require thousands of litres. Meanwhile, millions of tonnes of clothing are thrown away every year, much of it barely worn. Every time we buy something that already exists instead of something new, we reduce demand for production and keep a garment out of landfill for a little longer.

The second argument is economic. For families on limited incomes, second-hand clothing has always been a way to stretch the budget, and that remains true. But the market has also created new opportunities. Across Latin America, young entrepreneurs are running successful businesses on social media, selling carefully selected vintage pieces. Repair workshops and tailors, who were in danger of disappearing, are finding new customers who want to make their clothes last.

Critics raise some fair points. They argue that the growing popularity of second-hand shopping has pushed up prices, making it harder for poorer people to find affordable clothes. Others note that some wealthy countries export huge quantities of low-quality used clothing to Africa and Latin America, where much of it ends up as waste. These are real problems, and they deserve attention. However, they are arguments for regulating the trade better, not for abandoning the idea.

There is also a cultural change that we should not underestimate. Fast fashion has taught us to see clothes as disposable: something to wear twice, photograph and replace. Buying second-hand encourages a different relationship with what we own. When you find a well-made coat that has already lived one life, you are more likely to look after it, repair it and eventually pass it on.

Of course, nobody is suggesting that we should never buy anything new. Underwear, running shoes and certain work clothes are obvious exceptions. But if we made second-hand the first option rather than the last, the effect would be enormous. The most sustainable garment, as the saying goes, is the one that already exists.

title: La Pola: The Seamstress Who Became a Spy
paragraphs: In the centre of Bogotá, schoolchildren often stop in front of a statue of a young woman. Most of them know her simply as "La Pola". Her story is one of the best known in Colombian history, and yet, surprisingly, historians still disagree about some of its most basic facts, including her exact name and where she was born.

Policarpa Salavarrieta was probably born around 1795, most likely in the town of Guaduas, although some researchers believe she was born in Santafé, as Bogotá was then called. Some documents even suggest that her real name may have been Apolonia. What is certain is that her childhood was marked by tragedy: she lost both of her parents to a smallpox epidemic when she was still a young girl, and she was brought up partly by relatives in Guaduas.

As a young woman, she earned her living as a seamstress. It was a modest job, but it would turn out to be extremely useful. In 1816, Spanish troops had retaken control of New Granada after the first attempts at independence, and anyone suspected of supporting the patriot cause was persecuted. When La Pola moved to Santafé around this time, she offered her services in the homes of royalist families. While she sewed, she listened. Information about troop movements was passed on to the patriots, and she is also said to have helped young men escape the city to join the rebel army on the eastern plains.

Her activities could not remain secret forever. In 1817, a patriot messenger, Alejo Sabaraín, who according to many accounts was romantically involved with her, was captured carrying documents that revealed her role in the network. La Pola was arrested soon afterwards, tried and sentenced to death. On 14 November 1817, she was executed by firing squad in the city's main square. She was only about twenty-two years old.

Accounts of her final hours describe a woman who refused to show fear. She is said to have spoken out against the Spanish authorities and to have criticised the crowd for not resisting. Whether every detail of these accounts is accurate is impossible to know, as many of them were written years later by people who admired her.

Two years after her death, the patriot army won the decisive Battle of Boyacá, and New Granada became independent. La Pola, meanwhile, became a national symbol. Her face has appeared on banknotes and stamps, and the date of her execution, 14 November, is celebrated in Colombia as the Day of the Colombian Woman. For many, she represents the countless ordinary people, especially women, whose courage made independence possible.

title: Community Radio Finds New Listeners Online
paragraphs: For almost thirty years, Ventana Estéreo has been the voice of a small town of about eight thousand people in the mountains of Boyacá. From a tiny studio above a bakery, its volunteers have announced funerals, football results, lost cows and the price of potatoes. Now, the community station has found an unexpected way to reach a new generation of listeners: podcasts.

The project began two years ago, when the station's director, Hernando Suárez, noticed that young people in the town no longer listened to the radio. "They had their headphones on all the time, but they were listening to programmes from Mexico, Spain or the United States," he said. "Nobody was telling our own stories in the format they used." With a small grant from a cultural foundation and the help of two students from a nearby university, the station started recording short episodes that could be downloaded and listened to at any time.

The first series, "Voices of the Páramo", featured interviews with elderly farmers about how agriculture and the climate in the region had changed during their lifetimes. Each episode lasted around twenty minutes and was edited by teenagers from the local secondary school, who had been trained in sound production. To the team's surprise, the series was downloaded more than fifty thousand times, many of them by Colombians living abroad.

Since then, the station has produced podcasts on local legends, traditional recipes and the history of the town's football club. A series on mental health among rural young people, which was recorded with the support of a psychologist, has been particularly popular. Several episodes have been used by teachers in other regions as classroom material.

The success has brought new challenges. Producing podcasts takes far more time than live radio, and most of the team are still volunteers who have other jobs. The station's equipment is old, and internet connections in some rural areas are too slow for listeners to download episodes easily. "We are proud of what we have done, but enthusiasm alone doesn't pay the electricity bill," Suárez admitted.

Media researchers say that the case reflects a wider trend in Latin America, where community stations are increasingly combining traditional broadcasting with digital formats in order to survive. title: The Machine Will See You Now
paragraphs: Few decisions shape a life as profoundly as whether one is offered a job, and yet an increasing share of that decision is now delegated, at least in its early stages, to software. Applicant-tracking systems sift CVs for keywords; video platforms promise to infer "cultural fit" from facial expressions and tone of voice; gamified tests purport to measure traits such as risk tolerance and persistence. Proponents argue that such tools are faster, cheaper and, crucially, fairer than the human recruiters they supplement. It is this last claim that deserves closer scrutiny.

The case for automation is not without merit. Human judgement in hiring is notoriously unreliable. Recruiters, however well-intentioned, are swayed by an applicant's accent, surname, alma mater or even the firmness of a handshake. A system that evaluated every candidate against identical criteria would, in principle, strip away at least some of this arbitrariness. For a graduate from a provincial university in, say, Pasto or Montería, whose CV might once have been discarded unread by a recruiter in Bogotá, an algorithm indifferent to postcodes could open doors.

The difficulty lies in that qualifying phrase: in principle. Algorithms trained on historical data inherit the preferences embedded in that data. If a company has, over decades, predominantly promoted men from a handful of elite institutions, a model asked to identify "successful employees" will learn, without anyone instructing it to, that being male and having attended those institutions are markers of success. Far from eliminating bias, the system launders it, presenting yesterday's prejudice as today's objective calculation. Several large firms have reportedly abandoned recruitment tools for precisely this reason, though only after the damage had been done.

Compounding the problem is opacity. A rejected candidate can, at least in theory, ask a human interviewer why they were unsuccessful. Rarely, however, can a model offer an explanation that is both accurate and intelligible. Not only do applicants have no means of contesting a decision they do not understand, but employers themselves frequently have only a hazy grasp of how the tools they have purchased actually reach their conclusions. Accountability, in such circumstances, becomes diffuse to the point of disappearing: the vendor blames the data, the employer blames the vendor, and the candidate is left with an automated email.

None of this amounts to an argument for abandoning the technology altogether; that horse, as the saying goes, has long since bolted. What it does suggest is that the burden of proof should be reversed. Rather than assuming that automated systems are neutral until shown otherwise, regulators might require that they be independently audited for discriminatory outcomes before deployment, and periodically thereafter. Candidates should be told when an algorithm has played a substantial role in a decision and be given a meaningful route to human review. Some jurisdictions have begun to move in this direction; most, including much of Latin America, have yet to do so.

Ultimately, what is at stake is not merely efficiency but legitimacy. A hiring process is judged not only by whether it selects capable people, but by whether those it rejects can accept that they were treated fairly. A system that cannot explain itself may be quicker than a human recruiter; it is not, for that reason alone, more just. It is one thing to let machines help us decide; it is quite another to let them decide in our place while we look the other way.

title: The Sponge in the Clouds
paragraphs: Ask a resident of Bogotá where their tap water comes from and most will name a reservoir, a treatment plant, perhaps a river. Few will mention the páramo, the cold, misty, treeless grassland that stretches across the high Andes above the line where forests give way, typically somewhere between 3,000 and 4,500 metres. Yet it is to this improbable landscape, often dismissed as bleak and unproductive, that the capital owes the overwhelming majority of its drinking water. It is an ecosystem whose value is matched only by the degree to which it has been overlooked.

The páramo's hydrological role is less a matter of rainfall than of retention. Its soils, formed largely from volcanic ash and slowly decomposing vegetation, are extraordinarily rich in organic matter and remarkably porous; some can hold several times their own dry weight in water. Rather than allowing rain and fog to rush downhill in torrents, they absorb it and release it gradually, sustaining streams through the dry months. Hence the metaphor that has become almost obligatory in discussions of the subject: the páramo as a sponge. Remove the sponge, and a region that once enjoyed a steady supply is left alternating between floods and drought.

Central to this system are the frailejones, the silvery, rosette-shaped plants of the genus Espeletia that give many Colombian páramos their otherworldly appearance. Their leaves, covered in fine hairs, trap moisture from passing clouds, while the dead leaves that accumulate around their stems insulate them against nightly frosts. Such adaptations come at a cost: frailejones are thought to grow by only around a centimetre a year, which means that a specimen taller than an adult may well be older than the republic itself. Damage inflicted in an afternoon may take centuries to repair.

That damage is no longer hypothetical. Colombia is home to roughly half of the world's páramos, including Sumapaz, often described as the largest on the planet, and pressure on them has mounted for decades. Potato cultivation and cattle grazing have crept steadily uphill, compacting soils and stripping away vegetation. Mining has posed a still more acute threat; the long-running dispute over gold extraction in the Santurbán páramo, which supplies water to Bucaramanga, became a national cause célèbre. Overlaying all of these is climate change, which is pushing warmer conditions upslope and leaving species adapted to the cold with, quite literally, nowhere higher to go.

The legal response has been significant, if contested. Colombian law now prohibits mining and oil exploration within officially delimited páramos and restricts new agricultural activity. Yet the process of drawing those boundaries has proved fraught. Draw them too generously and thousands of small farmers, many of whose families have worked the land for generations, find their livelihoods suddenly illegal; draw them too narrowly and the protection becomes largely symbolic. Conservationists increasingly argue that the most durable solutions are those that treat páramo communities not as obstacles but as partners, compensating them for protecting the water on which millions downstream depend.

There is a broader lesson here about how societies value nature. The páramo produces no timber, attracts relatively few tourists and yields modest harvests. Its contribution is largely invisible, measured in what does not happen: the taps that do not run dry, the floods that do not come. It is precisely such quiet services that markets are worst at pricing and politicians most tempted to neglect, until, of course, the sponge has been wrung dry.

title: Against the Bucket List
paragraphs: Somewhere in a drawer, or more likely in a note on their phone, many people keep a list of places they intend to see before they die. Machu Picchu, the Northern Lights, Santorini at sunset, the salt flats of Uyuni: the entries vary less than one might expect. I should confess at the outset that I once kept such a list myself, and ticked off a respectable number of its entries. It is partly for that reason that I have come to regard the bucket list as one of the more quietly corrosive ideas in modern travel.

My first objection is that it turns places into trophies. The logic of the list is acquisitive: a destination is something one collects, verifies with a photograph and moves past. The question it encourages is not "What is this place like?" but "Have I done it?" One sees the consequences at any of the world's most photographed viewpoints, where visitors queue for the privilege of reproducing an image they have already seen thousands of times, spend a few minutes in front of the view itself, and leave. It is hard to imagine a less curious way of encountering the world.

My second objection concerns the places themselves. Because bucket lists are, by their nature, remarkably uniform, they concentrate millions of visitors on a small number of sites. The results are well documented: residents priced out of historic centres, fragile trails eroded beyond recognition, local economies reshaped around the demands of people who stay for forty-eight hours. Cities from Venice to Cartagena have experimented with entry fees, visitor caps and restrictions on holiday rentals, with varying degrees of success. Rarely, though, has anyone asked whether the list itself is part of the problem.

Defenders of the bucket list will say, not unreasonably, that it gives people something to aspire to; that for someone who grew up with little, standing at last before a wonder they had seen only in a schoolbook can be profoundly moving. I do not doubt it. Nor am I suggesting that anyone should be shamed for wanting to see the Iguazú Falls. My quarrel is not with the desire but with the framework, which converts a lifetime of potential discovery into a checklist compiled largely by marketing departments and algorithms.

What might replace it? Not, I think, a rival list of "hidden gems", which merely relocates the crowds; few phrases in travel writing have done more damage. Rather, a different habit of mind: going somewhere for a reason that is genuinely one's own, whether a book one loved, a dish one wants to learn to cook or a relative's village, and then staying long enough to be surprised. Some of the most memorable journeys I have taken were to places no list would include: a market town in Boyacá where I went to see a friend and stayed a week, and a grey port city in northern Portugal where it rained relentlessly and I have rarely been happier.

The bucket list promises that a life can be completed, its experiences ticked off one by one until nothing remains. Travel at its best suggests the opposite: that the world is inexhaustible, and that the point is not to finish it but to keep being changed by it. I deleted my list some years ago. I have not, so far, regretted it.

title: Threads of Memory: An Exhibition Review
paragraphs: It is a measure of how far the art world's hierarchies have shifted that an exhibition built largely around woven bags, blankets and hammocks should be one of the most talked-about shows of the season. "Threads of Memory", which runs until March at a converted colonial house in La Candelaria, brings together some two hundred textiles from across Colombia, from Wayuu mochilas to Andean ruanas, alongside work by a dozen contemporary artists for whom thread is not a craft material but a language. The result is uneven, occasionally frustrating, and frequently magnificent.

The opening rooms are the strongest. Here the curators have resisted the temptation to arrange objects by region or chronology, opting instead for themes: "Mourning", "Labour", "Exchange". The approach pays off. A Wayuu mochila, its geometric patterns encoding, we are told, motifs passed down through the female line, hangs a few feet from a contemporary installation made of thousands of strands of black thread, each knotted by relatives of people who disappeared during the armed conflict. Neither piece is diminished by the proximity; if anything, each sharpens our reading of the other. It is a quietly devastating juxtaposition, and one of several moments in which the exhibition achieves something close to revelation.

Equally welcome is the attention given to the weavers themselves. Too often, museum labels credit an indigenous object to an "anonymous artisan" while lavishing biographical detail on the urban artist hanging next to it. Here, wherever possible, makers are named, photographed and, in a series of short video interviews, allowed to speak about their work in their own words, several of them in Wayuunaiki with Spanish subtitles. The effect is to restore authorship to people from whom it has long been withheld.

The later rooms, however, lose their way. A section devoted to fashion, featuring garments by designers who have "collaborated" with weaving communities, feels less like an exhibition than a showroom, and conspicuously sidesteps the uncomfortable questions such collaborations raise about who profits and who receives credit. One cannot help suspecting the hand of a sponsor. The wall texts, too, become increasingly overwrought as the visitor progresses; by the final gallery, a perfectly straightforward blanket has been described as "a meditation on the porosity of time".

There are practical irritations as well. The house's narrow rooms struggle to cope with weekend crowds, and the lighting, kept low to protect the textiles, makes some labels all but illegible. The gift shop, mercifully, stocks pieces bought directly from weaving cooperatives rather than the usual mass-produced souvenirs. Visitors would be well advised to go on a weekday morning and to allow at least two hours.

These reservations should not deter anyone. At its best, "Threads of Memory" does what only the most ambitious exhibitions manage: it alters the categories through which we look. One leaves suspecting that the distinction between art and craft, so long taken for granted, was never much more than a matter of who was doing the making, and who was doing the deciding. That alone makes it essential viewing.

title: Why We Don't Save: A Conversation on Nudges
paragraphs: Why do people who sincerely intend to save money so often fail to do so? Behavioural economist Valentina Ruiz has spent fifteen years studying the gap between what we plan and what we do, working with banks, pension funds and governments across Latin America. We spoke to her about nudges, inertia and the limits of her own discipline.

Q: Let's start with the basics. Why is saving so hard? A: Because the costs are immediate and the benefits are distant, and human beings are not built to weigh those two things evenly. Economists call it present bias. If I offer you a nice dinner tonight or a slightly larger pension in thirty years, the dinner wins far more often than a purely rational calculation would predict. It's not that people are stupid or lazy. It's that the future self we are saving for feels, psychologically, a bit like a stranger.

Q: And this is where nudges come in? A: Exactly. A nudge is a change in the way a choice is presented that makes a particular option easier, without forbidding anything or significantly changing financial incentives. The best-known example is automatic enrolment. Traditionally, workers had to actively sign up for a pension plan, and huge numbers never got round to it. When you reverse the default, so that people are enrolled unless they choose to opt out, participation rates soar, in some studies from under half to over ninety per cent. Nobody is forced; inertia simply starts working for people rather than against them.

Q: Critics say that's manipulation. A: It's a fair concern, and I don't dismiss it. But there is no neutral way to design a form. If enrolment requires you to opt in, that is also a nudge, just one that happens to push people towards not saving. The real question is not whether to influence choices, since that is unavoidable, but in whose interest and how transparently. My own rule of thumb is that a nudge should be one you would be comfortable announcing publicly. If it only works because people don't notice it, something has gone wrong.

Q: Do nudges work as well in Latin America as in richer countries? A: Not always, and this is something my field has been slow to acknowledge. Many of the classic studies were conducted with salaried workers in the United States or Europe. In much of our region, around half the workforce is informal, without a regular payslip from which savings can be automatically deducted. You can't nudge someone into a system they aren't part of. Some of the most promising work here involves mobile phones, such as text reminders and digital savings "lockboxes" that people set up themselves, but the effects tend to be modest. We should be honest about that.

Q: So is behavioural economics overrated? A: I'd say it has occasionally been oversold. There was a period when some people spoke as if clever nudges could substitute for proper policy, as if you could fix inadequate pensions with better-designed letters. You can't. If wages are too low to save from, no amount of psychological insight will change that. Nudges are a useful tool, often cheap and sometimes remarkably effective, but they work best alongside structural reforms, not instead of them.

Q: Finally, do you follow your own advice? A: (Laughs.) Mostly. My savings are automatic, because I know perfectly well that I'd find a reason not to transfer the money every month. Knowing about bias doesn't make you immune to it. If anything, my research has made me more forgiving of other people's financial mistakes, and of my own.

title: Humboldt's Restless Eye
paragraphs: In June 1802, a small party of men struggled up the icy flanks of Chimborazo, the volcano in what is now Ecuador that was then believed to be the highest mountain in the world. Their feet were bleeding, several were suffering from altitude sickness, and a crevasse eventually blocked their path some way short of the summit. Yet the man leading them, a thirty-two-year-old Prussian named Alexander von Humboldt, paused repeatedly to do something his companions must have found baffling: he took out his instruments, measured the temperature, the air pressure and the boiling point of water, and noted which plants and insects could still be found at that altitude. It was entirely characteristic of him.

Born in Berlin in 1769 into a wealthy aristocratic family, Humboldt was expected to pursue a respectable career in the Prussian civil service. For a time he did, working as an inspector of mines, but his real passions lay elsewhere. He was voraciously curious about almost everything, from geology and botany to astronomy and anatomy, and he longed to travel. It was only after the death of his mother in 1796, which left him with a considerable inheritance, that he was in a position to fund an expedition of his own.

Having obtained, unusually, permission from the Spanish crown to explore its American colonies, Humboldt set sail in 1799 with the French botanist Aimé Bonpland. Over the following five years they travelled through present-day Venezuela, Cuba, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Mexico. They paddled up the Orinoco, confirming that a natural channel links it with the Amazon basin; they followed the Magdalena River towards Bogotá, where Humboldt spent time with the botanist José Celestino Mutis; and they crossed the Andes on foot, collecting tens of thousands of plant specimens along the way.

What set Humboldt apart was not simply the quantity of data he gathered but what he did with it. Whereas many naturalists of his day were content to name and classify species in isolation, he was interested in the connections between them. On Chimborazo he noticed that vegetation changed with altitude in distinct bands, much as it changed with latitude between the equator and the poles, and he went on to depict this in a celebrated cross-section of the mountain, labelling the plants found at each height. At Lake Valencia, in Venezuela, he observed that the clearing of forests had contributed to a fall in the lake's water level, and warned that human activity could alter the climate of a region. Rarely had anyone stated so clearly that nature was an interconnected whole, and that humans were capable of damaging it.

Back in Europe, Humboldt became arguably the most famous scientist of his age. His accounts of the journey were read by figures as different as Simón Bolívar, whom he is said to have met in Paris in 1804, and a young Charles Darwin, who took them with him aboard the Beagle. In his later years he attempted something even more ambitious: Kosmos, a multi-volume work intended to describe the entire physical universe as a unified system. He was still working on it when he died in 1859, at the age of eighty-nine.

Today Humboldt's name survives chiefly in geography, attached to a cold ocean current off the coast of Peru and to mountains, rivers and hundreds of species, while his ideas are largely taken for granted. Yet many of the concepts at the heart of modern ecology, from the interdependence of species to human-induced climate change, owe something to the restless man who stopped to measure the air on a mountain he could not climb.

title: Does Speaking Two Languages Train the Brain?
paragraphs: For much of the twentieth century, raising a child with two languages was widely regarded as a risk. Educators warned that bilingual children would become confused, fall behind their peers or end up speaking neither language properly, and some early studies appeared to confirm these fears. Those studies, it later emerged, had frequently compared bilingual children from poor immigrant families with monolingual children from wealthier backgrounds, attributing to language differences that were in fact the product of circumstance. By the end of the century, the pendulum had swung decisively the other way.

The new orthodoxy held that bilingualism not only did no harm but conferred a distinct cognitive advantage. The reasoning was elegant. Research suggested that a bilingual person's two languages are both active in the mind even when only one is being used, so the speaker must constantly suppress the irrelevant one. This continual act of selection, it was argued, amounted to a kind of workout for the brain's "executive functions", the set of abilities that allow us to focus attention, ignore distractions and switch between tasks. A series of experiments in which bilingual children and adults outperformed monolinguals on such tasks appeared to bear this out.

Even more striking were claims regarding old age. Studies of patients at memory clinics reported that bilinguals tended to show the symptoms of dementia several years later than monolinguals with comparable levels of brain deterioration, a finding interpreted as evidence of a "cognitive reserve" built up over a lifetime of juggling languages. Unsurprisingly, these results attracted enormous media attention, and the idea that learning a language could protect the ageing brain passed swiftly into popular wisdom.

It was not long, however, before doubts set in. When other research teams attempted to reproduce the executive-function findings with larger samples, many found no meaningful difference between bilinguals and monolinguals. One analysis suggested that studies supporting the advantage were considerably more likely to end up published than those that did not, a pattern that, if accurate, would have inflated the apparent strength of the effect. Critics also pointed out that "bilingual" covers an extraordinarily diverse population: a Colombian teenager who switches between Spanish and English on social media, an elderly Wayuu woman who speaks Wayuunaiki at home and Spanish at the market, and a Montreal civil servant who works in French and English lead very different linguistic lives. To expect a single, uniform effect across all of them may simply be naive.

The dementia research has proved similarly contested. Studies that follow large groups of healthy people over time, generally considered more reliable than those based on clinic patients, have produced mixed results, with some detecting a protective effect and others none at all. Disentangling bilingualism from factors such as education, income and immigration history remains notoriously difficult.

Where does this leave the would-be language learner? Arguably in a better position than the headlines implied. If the case for a dramatic, measurable boost to brainpower now looks shakier than it once did, the older fear that bilingualism causes harm has been comprehensively dismissed. And the most compelling reasons for learning a language were never neurological in the first place. Access to other people, other literatures and other ways of seeing the world hardly needs a brain scan to justify it.

title: Hybrid Work Three Years On
paragraphs: Executive summary. This report presents the findings of a survey of 340 organisations and 4,100 employees in Colombia, Peru and Chile, conducted by an independent research consultancy three years after most of the participating firms adopted hybrid working arrangements. Its purpose is to assess the effects of these arrangements on productivity, wellbeing, career development and organisational culture, and to offer recommendations to employers. Overall, the evidence suggests that hybrid work has become firmly established and is broadly valued by employees, but that its benefits are unevenly distributed and that several risks have so far received insufficient attention.

Productivity. Managers' assessments of productivity were largely positive, with 61 per cent reporting that output had remained stable and 24 per cent that it had improved. These figures should, however, be treated with caution, since few organisations had reliable baseline measures from before the transition, and self-reported assessments are prone to optimism. Where objective indicators were available, as in customer service and software development, the picture was more mixed: individual tasks requiring sustained concentration tended to benefit from remote days, whereas tasks relying on rapid informal collaboration often suffered.

Wellbeing. Employees overwhelmingly cited the reduction in commuting as the single greatest advantage; in the largest cities surveyed, respondents had previously spent an average of more than two hours a day travelling. Reported stress levels were lower among hybrid workers than among those required to attend the office full-time. Nonetheless, a significant minority, approximately one in five, reported difficulty separating work from home life, citing out-of-hours messages and a lack of suitable space. This problem was markedly more acute among younger employees living in shared accommodation and among women with caring responsibilities.

Career development. Perhaps the most concerning finding relates to progression. Employees who spent the majority of their time working remotely were less likely to have received a promotion or a significant new responsibility over the period than colleagues with comparable performance ratings who attended the office more frequently. While the data do not establish a causal relationship, they are consistent with the widely voiced concern that visibility continues to shape managers' judgements. Junior staff, moreover, reported fewer opportunities for informal learning, which had traditionally occurred through observing more experienced colleagues.

Organisational culture. Responses suggest that a sense of belonging has weakened in many organisations, particularly among employees who joined after the transition and have never experienced a full-time office environment. Firms that had established clear expectations, such as designated "anchor days" on which entire teams attend, reported notably higher levels of cohesion than those leaving attendance entirely to individual choice.

Recommendations. In light of these findings, organisations are advised to: (1) develop objective measures of performance that do not depend on physical presence; (2) introduce coordinated attendance days to support collaboration and mentoring; (3) adopt explicit policies on out-of-hours communication; and (4) monitor promotion data by work pattern in order to detect and correct any bias against remote workers. Further research is needed to establish the long-term effects of hybrid arrangements on careers, which may not become fully apparent for several more years.

title: Why Corrections Rarely Catch Up
paragraphs: Imagine a message that begins circulating in WhatsApp groups a few days before a local election. Citing an unnamed "official source", it claims that polling stations in certain neighbourhoods will be closed and that residents should vote elsewhere. Within hours, the electoral authorities and several news outlets have declared it false. The scenario is invented, but what tends to happen next is not. Weeks later, a surprising number of people will still recall the original claim, and some will still believe it, while far fewer will remember that it was ever corrected.

Why should corrections be so much less effective than the falsehoods they target? Part of the answer lies in speed and reach. One large study of social media found that false stories spread significantly faster and further than accurate ones, partly because they tended to be more novel and more emotionally charged, provoking surprise, fear or outrage. A correction, by contrast, is typically sober, qualified and, frankly, less interesting. It arrives later, travels through fewer channels and often fails to reach the very people who saw the original claim.

Even when a correction does reach its audience, the human mind does not simply delete the false information and replace it with the truth. Psychologists have described what they call the "continued influence effect": people who have been told that a piece of information is wrong frequently continue to rely on it when reasoning about events, particularly if the falsehood offered a neat causal explanation and the correction leaves an uncomfortable gap. Telling someone that a fire was not caused by faulty wiring is far less satisfying than telling them what did cause it.

Repetition compounds the problem. Studies have repeatedly shown that statements we have encountered before feel more true, regardless of their accuracy, simply because they are easier to process, a phenomenon known as the illusory truth effect. Paradoxically, this means that a correction which restates the myth prominently, as in the familiar headline format "Myth: X", may inadvertently reinforce the very claim it seeks to dispel.

There is, it should be said, some good news. The so-called "backfire effect", the idea that correcting people's beliefs causes them to cling to those beliefs even more strongly, attracted considerable attention a decade or so ago but has proved difficult to reproduce. Most of the time, corrections do shift beliefs in the right direction; they simply do so less completely and less durably than one might hope. Researchers have also had some success with "prebunking": warning people in advance about the techniques used to mislead them, such as fake experts or emotionally manipulative language, so that they are better equipped to recognise them when they appear.

For journalists and fact-checkers, the practical lessons are reasonably clear. Lead with the facts rather than the myth; offer an alternative explanation to fill the gap the falsehood leaves; keep corrections short and shareable; and, wherever possible, act before a claim has had time to take root. None of this guarantees that the truth will catch up. But it improves the odds in a race that, for the moment, the truth tends to lose.

title: The Interpreter
paragraphs: Marta had interpreted for presidents, surgeons and, once, memorably, a Nobel laureate who had fallen asleep halfway through his own speech. In twenty years she had learned that the booth was a kind of confessional in reverse: she was the one who spoke, and the words were never her own. She had made her peace with that long ago. It was, she told the trainees she occasionally mentored, the whole point.

The meeting in the community hall was a different matter. There was no booth, only a plastic chair at the end of a trestle table, a microphone that whistled whenever anyone leaned towards it, and some two hundred people seated on benches, many of whom had walked for hours. On one side of the table sat three executives from the mining company, flown in that morning; on the other, the leaders of the farmers' association, in their best shirts. Between them, quite literally, sat Marta.

For the first hour it went as these things usually go. The company's representative, a pleasant, silver-haired man called Whitfield, spoke of investment, jobs and "world-class environmental standards". Marta rendered it all into Spanish with the smooth neutrality she had spent a career perfecting. The farmers asked about the river. Whitfield assured them that the river would be monitored. They asked who would monitor it. He said it would be independent. They asked who would pay for it. There was a pause.

It was during that pause that Whitfield leaned towards his colleague and, apparently forgetting that the microphone was live, or perhaps forgetting that Marta existed, murmured, "They'll sign. They always sign in the end. It's just a question of how much."

Marta's training was unambiguous. An interpreter renders everything that is said in the room: not what was meant, not what ought to have been said, but what was said. She had once rebuked a junior colleague for softening a minister's insult. And yet, in the second or so before she spoke, she was aware of an entire life's worth of arguments assembling themselves. It was an aside, not part of the meeting. It would wreck the negotiations. It was not her place. Was it not, precisely, her place?
She translated it. Word for word, in the same even tone she had used for "world-class environmental standards".

The silence that followed was of a kind she had never encountered in a booth. Whitfield turned towards her with an expression not so much of anger as of genuine bewilderment, as though a piece of furniture had addressed him. Then an old woman near the front, who had not spoken all afternoon, began, very slowly, to laugh.

The meeting ended shortly afterwards. Marta was not invited back by the agency that had hired her, though no one ever said so explicitly; the calls simply became less frequent. She did not regret it, or told herself she did not. Years later, when trainees asked her about fidelity, she would tell them the rule was simple. What she did not tell them was how loud a single sentence can be, or how long a silence can last.

title: Microplastics Reach Remote Andean Lakes
paragraphs: Microscopic fragments of plastic have been detected in high-altitude lakes in the northern Andes, some of them in protected areas many kilometres from the nearest road, according to a study published this week by an international team of researchers. The findings add to a growing body of evidence that microplastic pollution, long associated with oceans and densely populated coastlines, has penetrated even the most apparently pristine environments on the planet.

The team collected water and sediment samples from fourteen glacial and páramo lakes in Colombia and Ecuador at altitudes ranging from 3,600 to 4,700 metres. Particles were identified in every lake sampled, albeit in widely varying concentrations. Each sample was filtered and examined under a microscope, and a subset of particles was analysed with infrared spectroscopy to confirm their composition. The majority consisted of fibres consistent with synthetic textiles such as polyester, alongside fragments of polyethylene and polypropylene, plastics commonly used in packaging.

How the particles arrived at such remote sites remains a matter of some debate. The researchers believe that atmospheric transport is the most plausible explanation: lightweight fibres, they suggest, may be lifted into the air from cities and agricultural areas in the valleys below, carried upslope by prevailing winds and deposited by rain, fog or snow. Lakes near popular trekking routes showed somewhat higher concentrations, pointing to a possible contribution from visitors' clothing and equipment, though the authors caution that the sample is too small to draw firm conclusions on this point.

"What struck us was not the quantity so much as the ubiquity," said the study's lead author, an environmental chemist. "We chose some of these sites precisely because we expected them to be clean, as a baseline. There is, it seems, no such thing as a baseline any more."

The ecological consequences are not yet well understood. High-altitude lakes support specialised communities of invertebrates and amphibians, several of which are already under pressure from rising temperatures and increased ultraviolet radiation. Laboratory studies have shown that microplastics can be ingested by small aquatic organisms and may act as carriers for other pollutants, but whether the concentrations observed in the Andes are sufficient to cause measurable harm remains an open question. Of particular interest to the region's authorities is the fact that several of the lakes sampled feed watercourses that eventually supply drinking water to Andean cities.

Independent scientists not involved in the study described it as a valuable contribution while noting its limitations. One pointed out that contamination of samples during collection and analysis is a persistent difficulty in microplastics research, since synthetic fibres are present in laboratory air and on researchers' own clothing. The authors say they took extensive precautions, including wearing cotton garments and using blank control samples, to minimise this risk.

The team now plans to install atmospheric collectors at several sites in order to measure deposition rates directly over a full year. Only then, they argue, will it be possible to identify where the particles are coming from, and therefore what might be done to reduce them.

title: Outwitting Procrastination: A Practical Guide
paragraphs: If you have ever reorganised your entire wardrobe rather than start a report due the next morning, you will know that procrastination is rarely a matter of not knowing what to do. Most procrastinators are perfectly aware of the task, the deadline and the consequences of missing it. What they lack is not information but a way of managing the discomfort the task provokes. That insight, now widely shared among psychologists who study the subject, is the starting point for this guide.

Understand what is really going on. It is tempting to regard procrastination as a failure of time management, to be cured with a better calendar app. Research increasingly suggests otherwise. Procrastination is better understood as a problem of emotion regulation: we put off tasks that make us feel anxious, bored, inadequate or overwhelmed, and the relief we experience when we turn to something more pleasant reinforces the habit. Seen in this light, the question is not "How do I find more time?" but "What exactly about this task am I trying to avoid?"

Shrink the first step. Large, vaguely defined tasks are particularly prone to being postponed, precisely because it is unclear where to begin. "Write the dissertation" is not a task; it is a source of dread. "Open the document and write three sentences about the methodology" is. Paradoxically, the less ambitious the first step, the more likely you are to take it, and once begun, tasks frequently turn out to be less unpleasant than anticipated. The hardest part, for most people, is the transition into the work, not the work itself.

Decide in advance when and where. One of the better-supported techniques in behavioural research involves forming what are known as implementation intentions: specific "if-then" plans that link a task to a particular situation. Rather than resolving vaguely to "study more this week", you might decide: "When I sit down in the library after lunch on Tuesday, I will spend forty minutes on past exam questions." By delegating the decision to a cue in the environment, you reduce the number of moments in which you must summon willpower.

Redesign your surroundings. Willpower is a notoriously unreliable resource, so it makes sense to rely on it as little as possible. If your phone is the principal source of distraction, place it in another room rather than merely turning it face down. Conversely, make the desired task as frictionless as you can: leave the relevant file open, the book on the desk, the running shoes by the door. Small obstacles matter far more than we like to admit.

Forgive yourself. This may be the least intuitive piece of advice, but it is supported by some intriguing evidence. In one study, university students who reported forgiving themselves for procrastinating before a first exam procrastinated less when preparing for the next one. Harsh self-criticism, it appears, simply adds to the negative emotions that drove the avoidance in the first place, setting up a vicious circle. Acknowledging the lapse and moving on is not complacency; it is strategy.

Finally, a word of realism. None of these techniques will turn a lifelong procrastinator into a model of efficiency overnight, and occasional delay is a normal part of being human. Where procrastination is chronic and accompanied by persistent low mood or anxiety, it may be worth speaking to a professional. For most of us, however, the aim is not perfection but progress: fewer wasted evenings, and a little less dread.

title: A Year Without a Car in Bogotá
paragraphs: Twelve months ago, after the third time in a fortnight that I sat motionless on the Avenida Boyacá for forty minutes, listening to the same radio advert for a dental clinic, I sold my car. Friends reacted as though I had announced I was joining a monastery. "In Bogotá?" one of them asked, in the tone people normally reserve for news of a serious illness. What follows is not a manifesto, merely an honest account of what the year has actually been like.

Let me begin with a confession that will cost me any credibility with cycling purists: I did not, at first, enjoy it. Bogotá sits at around 2,600 metres, and my lungs, accustomed to the sedentary comfort of a driver's seat, made their feelings known on every incline. The afternoon rains, which arrive with the punctuality the buses lack, soaked me with dispiriting regularity until I finally invested in waterproofs that did not make me look like a large blue tent. And I had underestimated how much of the city's cycling infrastructure consists of lanes that end abruptly, as if the planners had lost interest halfway through a sentence.

Somewhere around the third month, however, something shifted. My commute, which had been a daily exercise in suppressed rage, became, if not exactly pleasant, then at least predictable: thirty-five minutes, give or take, regardless of traffic. I began to notice the city in a way that is impossible through a windscreen: the man who sells arepas outside the same bakery every morning, the jacarandas on a side street in Teusaquillo, the precise point at which the smell of eucalyptus gives way to diesel. I also, somewhat to my irritation, became fitter than I have been since university.

Sundays were a revelation. I had always known about the Ciclovía, the weekly closure of more than a hundred kilometres of main roads to motor traffic, but as a driver I had experienced it chiefly as an inconvenience. Joining it was something else entirely: grandmothers on rollerblades, toddlers on balance bikes, aerobics instructors bellowing through loudspeakers in car parks. For a few hours, a city often described as chaotic and hostile becomes something closer to a village fête with a million guests.

I would be misleading you, though, if I implied that car-free life is uniformly idyllic. My bicycle was stolen in June from a supposedly secure car park, and its replacement now spends its nights in my flat. Some trips remain unfeasible without a taxi, particularly late at night or in areas where the roads are frankly too dangerous to cycle. And I am acutely aware that my experience is that of a reasonably fit, middle-class man living in the north of the city, within reach of a TransMilenio station. For many residents of the southern periphery, who already travel two hours each way by bus, "giving up the car" is not a lifestyle choice but an everyday reality without any of the romance.

Would I go back? Financially, the answer is an emphatic no: between fuel, insurance, parking and repairs, I have saved a sum I am almost embarrassed to disclose. Beyond that, I find I no longer think about it, which is perhaps the most telling result of all. The car, which once seemed indispensable, has simply ceased to be part of the question.
